source.title: Can Large Language Models Reinvent Foundational Algorithms?
source.authors: Jian Zhao; Haoren Luo; Yu Wang; Yuhan Cao; Pingyue Sheng; Tianxing He

page_placements.theme: Non-propagation to related, implied or multi-hop facts; target inferable from retained knowledge

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. It includes appendices and quoted evaluation-prompt templates.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses its own GRPO-based unlearning intervention and measures whether target algorithms can be recovered in coding tasks, with and without algorithmic hints. This conceptually tests recovery after knowledge suppression, but not the specific fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompt-attack recipes in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study tests recovery after suppressing algorithm knowledge, not recovery through unrelated-data fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, or quantization. It does test recovery with explicit high-level and step-by-step algorithmic hints. Aggregate recovery rates and forgetting rates are reported directly; detailed per-algorithm cells are not reproduced here. The name-suppression experiment is a separate intervention and is not counted as a claim-version result because it suppresses names without unlearning and does not test the listed recovery attacks.
record.test_reason: The study uses GRPO-based unlearning as a tool to suppress recall so it can ask whether LLMs can reinvent foundational algorithms. Forgetting rate and LCB/AIME25 utility (Table 3) are its own intervention's performance. The recovery measure cannot separate residual hidden knowledge from fresh reinvention: the authors treat recovery as an upper bound on reinvention, not as evidence of shallow unlearning. The level-1 and level-2 hints describe the target algorithm itself, so success under them is instruction-following, not elicitation of suppressed knowledge. No fine-tuning, activation, quantization, paraphrase, jailbreak or other attack is applied to test whether unlearning holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that nearly half of the target algorithms (9 of 20) are not recovered without hints, and that name-token suppression alone cuts recovery. They add that hints narrow the gap, and that verifier feedback sustains reasoning but does not expand coverage. They frame unlearned recovery as an approximate upper bound on reinvention, noting unlearning may not fully remove knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GRPO-based on-policy unlearning with a refusal-style cold-start SFT stage and retain data; this is not the gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU recipe named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery changes with model, hint level, and verifier setting. The paper reports that name-token suppression also changes recovery, but that intervention is not an unlearning attack test.

fits_no_version.finding: After unlearning, with judge-scored forgetting rates of 90–96%, models still solve no-hint application tasks needing the target algorithm at 6.6–35.2% average RR. Coverage is 30–55% of algorithms, versus 85–100% for the original models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearned models that fail concept-level probes can still apply the target algorithm in downstream tasks; this may reflect residual knowledge or reinvention.

record.problems: The authors state that unlearning does not guarantee equivalence to retraining without target knowledge. The study covers a limited set of models and algorithms; each model–algorithm pair has a single unlearning run, with no variability across independent training runs. Recovery uses an application-task benchmark and algorithmic hints, not the specified recovery attacks.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 4 report per-algorithm recovery rates and coverage by model and hint level; Table 3 reports per-algorithm forgetting rates and utility. Those cells are omitted in favor of the explicitly reported aggregate rows, not averaged anew.

untested.parts: No simple attack is applied to test whether the unlearned knowledge is recoverable; only the method's own forgetting probes and utility are reported.
No activation ablation or internal analysis.
No paraphrase, jailbreak, language or in-context attack; the hints describe the target algorithm itself.
The GRPO unlearning is not evaluated against any of the recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. Unlearning is the experimental instrument for a reinvention question, not the object of study. The reader's E labels are dropped because the hints contain the target algorithm. The A label is dropped because no attack on the unlearning is run and the no-hint recovery is ambiguous. The name-suppression experiment is decoding-time masking without weight updates and is correctly excluded. Single unlearning run per model-algorithm pair.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests recovery after its own GRPO-based unlearning in application tasks without hints, alongside forgetting-rate probes and retained utility. It does not test whether the listed simple attacks recover knowledge, nor compare with a model retrained without the target knowledge.
No recovery fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or subset-of-facts examples.
No activation-direction ablation or internal edit to test access-blocking versus deletion.
The study tests explicit high-level and step-by-step algorithmic hints, not paraphrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or other prompt-only attacks.
No newer counter-method is tested for resistance to the attacks listed in the claim.

relation.reason: The unlearning is an instrument for the reinvention question. The study does not test whether unlearning is shallow or whether attacks recover the knowledge.

tranche.reason: Uses GRPO unlearning as a tool to suppress recall and reports its own method's forgetting rate and utility (Table 3). Recovery is measured as reinvention on application tasks, not as an attack on unlearned knowledge.

source_check.notes: All six rows match Tables 1, 3 and 4 and are correctly linked to no version. No-hint RR after unlearning mixes residual knowledge with fresh reinvention; the authors treat it as an approximate upper bound on reinvention, not as leakage. Forget-set queries are concept-level only, and application tasks are excluded from unlearning data. Table 3 text is flattened, but the Average and Origin rows place correctly.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: No-hint application-task recovery across the three unlearned models
reader_labels.reason: Recovery remains nonzero and varies substantially by model (30.1%, 6.6%, and 35.2%), despite high forgetting-probe rates; the task is recovery, not one of the specified attacks (rr-qwen-thinking-nohint, rr-qwen-instruct-nohint, rr-gemma-nohint, fr-qwen-thinking, fr-qwen-instruct, fr-gemma).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Explicit algorithmic hints across the three unlearned models
reader_labels.reason: High-level and especially step-by-step hints increase aggregate recovery over no-hint recovery for the unlearned models; the study reports average RR by hint level (rr-qwen-thinking-nohint, rr-qwen-thinking-level1, rr-qwen-thinking-level2, rr-qwen-instruct-nohint, rr-qwen-instruct-level1, rr-qwen-instruct-level2, rr-gemma-nohint, rr-gemma-level1, rr-gemma-level2).
